maya: Quick thread — RFC follow-up: supporting long-lived KV scan cursors (iterators) while still allowing aggressive eviction/shard handoff. TL;DR: product needs cursor semantics for analytics pipelines; runtime needs to reclaim memory. Tradeoffs?

jules: We discussed cursors briefly in the snapshot RFC but didn't land on semantics. Do we want snapshot-isolated cursors (pin everything they touch) or cheap cursors that can transparently rehydrate?

kevin: Pinning is impossible at scale (hot analytics jobs hold prefixes for minutes). We need a mechanism that lets a cursor resume even if its prefix was evicted or moved. That implies some durable compact snapshot or reapply path.

samir: +1. Two high-level options: 1) Cursor-level MVCC snapshot stored in object store (S3) when cursor duration > threshold. 2) Cursor resilience via resumable reads: keep sequence token + oplog window and allow the cursor to request replay from another node.

maya: Product requirement: customers expect "stable scan" semantics for export/backup jobs — they want no duplicates and no missing rows across a scan. We can accept eventual consistency if we document, but many will require linearizable iteration.

jules: If we aim for linearizable iteration we must either: a) prevent evict of touched keys until scan complete (pin), b) create a read-stable layer that materializes results. Pinning = huge mem cost. Materialize = storage + I/O cost.

kevin: There's also a hybrid: soft-pin + async materialize. Soft-pin reserves a tiny token and lets eviction proceed but keeps a short lived tombstone that allows a rehydrate RPC to fetch required values from backing store or from write-ahead log. Basically: evict but keep a compact resurrection pointer (seq range + owner node).

samir: Pros/cons: soft-pin keeps memory low, but correctness depends on retention of sufficient history (oplog or S3 snapshots). If we rely on oplog, need cross-node durable replication of recent ops and gapped retention windows will break resumes.

kevin: Implementation sketch for soft-pin resumable cursor: 
- Cursor open request -> runtime returns cursor-id + stable-cut (txn epoch / seq)
- When eviction runs, if prefix has active cursors, we emit a lightweight resurrection token: {cursor_ids: [id], stable_cut: X, writer_epoch, owner_node}
- On cursor next() and miss, client asks runtime to rehydrate using token -> runtime replays ops from stable_cut..now (from local cache or remote owner) and streams missing rows.

maya: Important: we must guarantee no duplicates across rehydrate/replay. So cursor must be able to ack last-seen position and runtime must start replay strictly after that position.

jules: Also need to think about multi-tenant fairness: hot scan jobs shouldn't prevent eviction for regular traffic. So soft-pin tokens must have TTL + token priority. If token TTL expires, resume fails with a clear error telling client to either restart scan (best-effort snapshot) or switch to materialized snapshot path.

kevin: Metrics we should track: active-cursor-count, total-resurrects, rehydrate-latency (p95), rehydrate-failures (expired token), memory-saved-by-soft-pin. Also track per-tenant ephemeral-snapshot-storage bytes if we use S3 fallback.

samir: Edge case: what if prefix moved to another node and owner node's oplog segment already compacted? We need cross-node durability. Two approaches: (1) short-term replication of recent oplog segments to ring peers, or (2) force rehydrate to go to object-store snapshot. Replication increases network+mem cost but lower latency; object-store is slower but cheap.

maya: Product input: customers will prefer faster resume over cost for dashboards, but for nightly exports they accept slower S3-backed path. So expose policy: cursor_policy: {durability: "low|standard|high", retention_secs: N}. Default standard = soft-pin + short oplog replication (60s) + S3 fallback for >5m scans.

jules: API surface: POST /v1/cursors -> {prefix, policy} -> returns {cursor_id, stable_cut, token, estimated_cost}. GET /v1/cursors/:id/next?block=true -> returns rows or 410 if token expired with error payload: {retry_suggestion: "materialize"}.

kevin: Security: cursor tokens must be bound to auth context (token can't be used cross-tenant), and to a client nonce to avoid accidental reuse when a crash happens. Also TTLs encrypted server-side.

maya: Operational concerns: we must add a new eviction check path to consult cursor index; this is a small in-memory map keyed by prefix -> cursor-count. Must avoid global locks. Use sharded cursor maps colocated with eviction worker.

samir: Back-of-envelope: if we keep only tokens (no values) memory overhead is tiny: 64 bytes * active cursors. But oplog replication PV will add ~R bytes/s per shard. Need to instrument.

jules: Failure modes: 
- Token expired mid-scan -> client gets 410, resume requires starting from last checkpoint or materializing snapshot.
- Replay gap due to compaction -> error upstream indicating compaction boundary.
- Large fan-out (many cursors on same prefix) -> add rate limiting and recommend server-side materialize.

maya: Action items: 
- Engineering spike: implement soft-pin token + repro of rehydrate flow (owner node replay) - samir + kevin (1 week)
- API draft for cursor_policy and error codes - maya + jules (3 days)
- Perf model: cost of oplog replication vs S3 materialize - kevin (2d)

kevin: I'll stub out an internal design doc. Quick pseudo: 
```
// cursor token
struct CursorToken { uuid, prefix, stable_cut, owner_node, expires_at, auth_sig }

// rehydrate flow
client.next(cursor_id) -> node A miss -> node A calls node B: /rehydrate?token=...&from_seq=last_seen+1 -> node B streams ops -> node A applies to iterator and responds
```

jules: One more: for linearizability we must be careful about concurrent writes while replaying. The replayed ops should be strictly ordered before any new ops at >now, and clients should see consistent order. Using stable_cut and strictly replaying up to live seq works.

maya: Sounds good. If spike goes well, we can ship beta behind a feature flag and add telemetry. Thanks all. :thumbsup:
